reading.identification: Mid-19th-century Ghent townhouse on the east side of the Korenmarkt: a narrow (7.8 m) four-storey burgher house in painted cement render over a full-width commercial ground floor (restaurant/fast-food unit with fascia signage and pavement terrace), with wrought-iron Juliet balconettes to the upper windows and a slate pitched roof running parallel to the square.
reading.notes:
IDENTITY CAVEAT: the magenta box in B/0 straddles a party joint between two near-identical rendered houses (the "...ville" unit and the Pizza Hut unit). Both are the same type and period, so this grammar holds for either; do not treat the box edges as the party walls.

STOREYS: marked inferred, not seen. B/0 clearly shows the ground floor plus three upper window rows, but the top of the facade is clipped in both street photos and the set A tile has a duplicated-band render glitch straight through the facade, so I cannot count the top row directly. 4 storeys reconciles the visible rows with the 17.1 m measured height: 4.2 ground + 3 x 3.1 upper = 13.5 m of wall, leaving 3.6 m eaves-to-ridge, right for a ~45 deg pitch on a 7.8 m span. If the generator needs a fallback, 5 storeys at 2.8 m with a shallower roof is the only competing reading.

ROOF: read from set A, which is the right source for massing. The roof zone at the top of the box is clean of the glitch and shows a slate-grey pitched plane with a street-parallel eaves line and light dormer patches along the row. B/1 shows a red pantile eave inside the box on a neighbour, so the row is mixed slate/pantile — vary tile colour along the terrace rather than making the whole row uniform. A mansard is the plausible alternative if the generator has one; the lower slope in the tile is steep.

MATERIAL, and what to keep out of geometry: the wall is smooth painted cement render (anthracite/charcoal grey), NOT brick. At 3x in B/0 there is no bond pattern and no joint shadow, only a flat painted surface with rain-streak staining below the ledges. So concrete is the dielectric class and roughness stays low — 1.2 mm RMS, i.e. a smooth painted surface with age, nowhere near the 3-8 mm of exposed brick. Do not mesh the render texture or the staining.

TRIM SPLIT — important, one enum value cannot carry this: window frames are white painted timber/PVC (wood is the correct dielectric class, which is why trim=wood), but three elements on this facade are genuinely metal and should be assigned metal separately if the generator supports it: (a) the wrought-iron Juliet balustrades, (b) the shopfront framing and fascia, (c) the projecting box sign brackets. Sills, surrounds and the string course are painted render/stone, i.e. concrete. Getting the sills wrong as metal would over-reflect a lot of small horizontal area.

WHAT TO SPEND GEOMETRY ON (>10 cm regime, this is where the 28 GHz street-level field is decided): the Juliet balconettes are the defining feature and project roughly 10-15 cm with open scrollwork — model them as real facets, they sit directly at first/second floor and will dominate off-specular scatter down onto the pavement. Then the projecting sills, the string course above the shop fascia, the eaves cornice, and the window reveals (shallow class, ~0.12 m — B/0 shows jamb shadow but reference imagery cannot resolve depth better than a class, so do not invent a number). The ironwork is thin-bar: keep it as bars, not a solid panel, or it becomes a mirror it is not.

WHAT MUST STAY A NUMBER (1-10 cm regime): render texture, the fascia lettering, the sign graphics, the window decals. These are roughness and scattering coefficient only. Meshing them produces specular garbage.

GROUND FLOOR: dark-framed full-height glazing with a solid fascia band above and a recessed entry — classed shopfront rather than cafe_glazing because of the fascia and the retail-style stallriser framing, but the unit functions as a restaurant. Large flat glass panes at eye level: this is the single most radio-significant surface on the building and deserves the finest facet budget, along with the balconettes.

CLUTTER — calibrate to this street, do not apply a generic rule: fronting_street is highway=pedestrian, car_access=none, surface=paving_stones, distance 0.0 m. NO PARKED CARS, NO MOVING VEHICLES. What the photos actually show on this pavement: cafe terrace tables and stacked metal chairs, tall black market-parasols, A-board menu boards, a wooden terrace enclosure with planting, a parked scooter and bicycles, tram rails and overhead catenary wires in the carriageway, and dense pedestrian traffic. The catenary wires are worth including — they are metal, they cross the corridor, and nothing else in the scene is at that height.

SECOND FRONTAGE: street_frontages=2 with 4 attached neighbours means this is a corner unit. The return elevation should carry the same render, sill and cornice grammar but with a sparser and more irregular bay rhythm, and a largely blank or service-doored ground floor rather than a second shopfront.
